subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 00min

periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write about special events and activities that take place at their school on Republic Day (p. 76)
periods.implied_lo: Students can connect a national symbol's visual features to the civic values those features represent.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you had to explain to a younger child why we raise the flag on this day, what would you say?' Prompt students who struggle to look back at the colour meanings they just read. Keep sharing unhurried — the quality of the connection matters more than the number of responses collected.
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the tricolour flag with colour labels

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share what they recall of their school's last Republic Day celebration — what they saw, heard, and felt standing near the flagpole. A few volunteers describe their memory; teacher draws out the flag's three colours on the board without yet naming their significance.

Class opens Textbook p. 76 together. Teacher reads the passage aloud, pausing after each colour to ask: 'What does this colour remind you of in everyday life?' Students connect saffron, white, and green to concrete examples from their surroundings. The Ashoka Chakra's place on the white band is noted and discussed briefly.

Students write individually in their notebooks, responding to the Textbook p. 76 prompt about special Republic Day events at their school. Teacher moves around the room, nudging students to include at least one detail about the flag or National Anthem from the passage they just read.

Three or four students read out their responses. Class discusses: why might all schools across India do similar things on this day? Teacher closes by asking students to hold one word in mind — the word 'Constitution' — without explaining it yet, leaving natural curiosity for the content that follows in this section.

periods.section_context: Republic Day school celebration, tricolour flag colours (saffron, white, green), Ashoka Chakra, National Anthem, Republic Day 26 January 1950.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write down five rules followed at school and propose one new rule they would make (p. 79)
periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the purpose of shared rules to the functioning of a community or institution.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Gandhi ji kept strict cleanliness rules in his ashram — why do you think he believed rules about small everyday things mattered?' This draws out the link between civic values and everyday behaviour. For the group activity, ensure mixed groups so that students from different backgrounds contribute different rule-experiences.
materials: Strips of chart paper (one per group)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the short passage in the textbook connecting India's independence from British rule to the need for a Constitution — a shared set of rules for the country. Students are asked: 'What would happen in your classroom if there were no rules at all?' A quick open discussion follows, with the teacher noting responses on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 79 and work individually to list five rules actually followed at their school. Teacher prompts: 'Think about rules for the classroom, the corridor, the playground, the library.' After listing, each student writes one new rule they would introduce and gives a reason for it.

Students share in small groups of four. Each group chooses the two rules they find most important and writes them on a strip of chart paper. Groups then share with the class; teacher guides a brief discussion on whether rules protect everyone equally — connecting school rules to the idea of constitutional values without using that word.

Teacher invites a brief reflection: 'Is there a rule at school that you think is unfair? How might you try to change it through the right channels — talking to a teacher, writing a suggestion?' This links civic behaviour to the Constitution's purpose. Students jot one sentence in their notebooks summarising why rules matter.

periods.section_context: India's Constitution as governing rules, Independence Day and Republic Day distinction, school rules, civic norms and their purpose.

periods.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students observe an Indian currency note carefully and fill in the observation table (p. 80)
periods.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations of an everyday object and explain the civic or historical meaning of its design features.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Gandhi ji had strict rules about cleanliness in his ashram — how does that connect to the symbol we see on the note today?' This surfaces the link between traditional values and modern civic policy naturally. If some pairs do not have a real note, the textbook figure on p. 80 is a complete substitute.
periods.activity_title: A Currency Note Under the Lens
materials: One Indian currency note per pair (any denomination brought safely)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the annotated currency note showing Mahatma Gandhi's portrait, National Emblem, and Swachh Bharat symbol

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a currency note (or points to the textbook figure) and asks: 'You have handled this many times — what is printed on it?' Students call out observations freely. Teacher lists responses on the board without judging or correcting — this reveals what students already notice versus what they overlook.

Working in pairs, students place a real currency note beside Textbook p. 80 and systematically fill in the observation table — recording denomination, dominant colour, languages visible, monument or animal depicted, and any other symbol. Teacher circulates, drawing attention to the spectacles symbol and the raised dots for visually impaired users, asking: 'Why would a currency note need to be 'readable' by touch?'

Class compares findings across different denominations — teacher builds a simple board table showing what different groups found on notes of different values. The National Emblem (three lions) and its connection to the Ashoka Chakra on the flag, already encountered in the previous unit of work on the tricolour, is noted as a recurring symbol.

Teacher explains the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol and its link to Gandhi ji's values of cleanliness and public responsibility. Students write one observation in their notebook: one thing on the note they had never noticed before, and what they now understand it means.

periods.section_context: Indian currency note observation table: denomination, colour, Mahatma Gandhi portrait, National Emblem (three lions), Ashoka Chakra, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol, raised prints for visually impaired, monuments and animals on notes.

periods.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students design an emblem for their school using symbols, words, shapes, and colours to convey a chosen message (p. 82)
periods.implied_lo: Students can create a symbol-based design that communicates a chosen value or identity through deliberate use of visual elements.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Would you choose a plant, a bird, or a geometric shape — and why does that choice say something about your school?' Encourage students to consider natural elements from the school's own surroundings rather than copying national symbols. Allow an unhurried drawing phase so the thinking behind the design is genuinely the student's own.
materials: Drawing paper or blank notebook page
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the National Emblem (Ashoka lion capital) for reference

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the National Emblem discussion from the previous work on currency notes, asking: 'What message do three lions standing together send?' Students then look at Textbook p. 82 together and discuss what makes an emblem different from a simple picture — it carries a meaning, uses symbols deliberately, and represents a community.

Students work individually on Textbook p. 82's task: designing a school emblem. They first jot down in a corner of their paper: (a) one value or quality they want the emblem to show, (b) one natural element from near the school they could use, and (c) a short motto of three to five words. Only then do they begin drawing and colouring the emblem itself.

Students share their emblems with a partner, explaining the meaning behind each symbol, colour, and word they chose. Partners give one warm feedback ('I like how you…') and one wondering ('I wonder why you chose…'). A few pairs share briefly with the whole class.

Teacher closes by noting how national and state emblems grow from the same process — choosing what a community values and expressing it through symbols. Students label their emblem designs with their name for display.

periods.section_context: National Emblem (three lions) as model, school emblem design using symbols, colours, shapes, and a motto to express a school community value.

periods.textbook_anchor: Symbols that Speak — Students find out the state animal, bird, tree, and flower of their own state with the teacher's help (p. 83)
periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a guided inquiry to gather specific information and connect findings to a broader environmental or civic question.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you or your family ever seen a peacock or a tiger in the wild or near your village? Where?' This draws out local ecological knowledge. If students' state has a particularly well-known conservation story for its state animal or bird, invite a student to share what they know before the teacher adds detail.
materials: Reference chart or printed list of state symbols (provided by teacher)
India map poster or textbook map (optional)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures of tiger and peacock alongside the riddle text

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the riddles from Textbook p. 83 aloud without naming the answers — students guess the national animal and national bird through the clues given. After the answers are revealed, teacher asks: 'Why do you think India chose the tiger and not the lion as its national animal, even though three lions appear on the National Emblem?' This prompts genuine thinking about conservation and ecology.

Students open Textbook p. 83 and undertake the inquiry task: using the reference chart provided by the teacher, they fill in the four state symbols of their own state (animal, bird, tree, flower). Teacher circulates and, for each symbol, asks students to say one fact they know about that plant or animal from their own experience or locality.

Students work in pairs: each pair picks one of their state symbols and finds out (using the reference chart or teacher guidance) where in the state that animal or bird is commonly found, and whether it faces any threat. Pairs report back orally — teacher builds a brief class list on the board linking each symbol to a habitat or conservation note.

Teacher draws the session to a close by connecting state symbols to national ones: 'Lions that once lived widely across India now survive only in Gir forest in Gujarat — their protection became urgent enough that it shaped the national choice of symbols.' Students note one new fact they learned about a national or state symbol in their notebooks.

periods.section_context: National Animal (tiger), National Bird (peacock), riddles to identify national symbols, lions in Gir forest conservation, state symbols (animal, bird, tree, flower) inquiry.

periods.textbook_anchor: Our Vibrant Culture — Students find out about languages spoken by classmates and then learn what a chosen word is called in different languages (p. 84)
periods.implied_lo: Students can gather linguistic data from peers and use it to describe cultural diversity within their immediate environment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do any of you know a song, a lullaby, or a proverb in a language other than the one we use in class — where did you learn it?' Folk songs and oral traditions surfaced here reflect the content's emphasis on languages carrying history and stories. Ensure every student's home language is represented and respected equally on the word-wall.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks the class: 'How many languages are spoken in the homes of students sitting in this very room?' A quick show of hands for each language students know at home — teacher tallies on the board. Students then open Textbook p. 84 and read the passage about India's thousand-plus languages and the word 'Māmpalam' for mango in Tamil.

The class carries out the Textbook p. 84 activity together: each student who knows a language other than the medium of instruction contributes the word for 'mango' (or another agreed common word) in their home language. Teacher writes each word on the board in that language's script if possible, or in Roman transliteration, building a class multilingual word-wall.

Students discuss in pairs: 'What does it tell us that the same fruit has so many different beautiful names?' Then the class discusses: how does knowing even one word of another language change how you feel about the person who speaks it? Teacher notes that digital translation apps now make cross-language curiosity easier to pursue at home.

Students write in their notebooks: the word-wall entry for their own language, plus two words from languages they did not know before this discussion. Teacher closes by asking: 'India's diversity of languages grew over thousands of years — does that feel like a problem to you, or a strength?' Students share one-word answers to end the unit.

periods.section_context: India's 1000-plus languages, 'mango' as a word in Tamil (Māmpalam) and other languages, class language survey, multilingual word-wall, digital translation tools.

periods.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — In small groups, students use a dupatta or scarf to help each other make a traditional headgear (p. 87)
periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a regional craft or clothing tradition reflects the cultural identity and environment of the community it comes from.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone's family have a headgear tradition — for a wedding, a festival, or a particular community occasion?' Students from communities with living headgear traditions become the experts here. Ensure the group composition is mixed so that this sharing crosses community lines within the class.
materials: One dupatta or scarf per group of four
periods.visual_aids: Textbook photographs of saafa/pagri from Rajasthan and topi from Himachal Pradesh

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to the photographs of regional headgear and asks: 'Where have you seen headgear like this — at a wedding, a fair, in a film?' Students share briefly. Teacher introduces the forest-garden metaphor from Textbook p. 86: 'A forest with many kinds of trees is stronger than a garden with only one — how might that idea apply to India's diversity of traditions?'

Students form groups of four. Following Textbook p. 87's activity, each group uses a dupatta or scarf to attempt tying a simple traditional headgear style shown in the textbook. Group members take turns helping each other — the process of adjusting and retying is itself the learning. Teacher circulates, noting which groups are collaborating and naming that collaboration explicitly.

Each group discusses: 'In what situations would this headgear be worn — everyday work, a festival, a formal ceremony?' Groups then briefly share one observation about how the headgear connects to climate or occasion (e.g., a wrapped pagri protecting from desert sun). Teacher notes that craft traditions like headgear-making are passed down through families and communities over generations.

Students each write one sentence in their notebooks: what their headgear-making attempt taught them about a regional tradition they had not thought about before. Teacher closes by asking: 'If this tradition disappeared, what would be lost?' — a gentle prompt toward valuing cultural heritage.

periods.section_context: Forest-garden diversity metaphor, saafa/pagri (Rajasthan), topi (Himachal Pradesh), dupatta/scarf headgear-making activity, headgear at weddings and formal occasions, craft traditions passed through communities.

periods.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students identify and mark on an India map the states where classical dance forms originated (p. 89)
periods.implied_lo: Students can read a political map of India to locate and record the regional origins of cultural practices.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you find your own state on the map — does it have a dance form listed? If not, does it mean your state has no dance tradition?' This prevents the misconception that only listed classical forms are valid, and opens space for students to name folk forms from their own region. Keep the map-marking activity moving steadily so all dance forms are located before discussion begins.
materials: Printed outline map of India (one per student)
Reference list of dance forms and their states of origin (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of India showing state boundaries; textbook images of classical dance forms

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads out three or four dance form names from the textbook — Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi — and asks: 'Have you seen any of these performed, on television, at a festival, or at school?' Students share briefly. Teacher then asks: 'If each dance form grew in a particular part of India, what might that tell us about how culture develops differently in different places?'

Students open Textbook p. 89 and, guided by the teacher's reference list, mark and label the states of origin of the classical dance forms shown on their outline map of India. They use different colours for different dance forms. Teacher circulates, asking individual students to read a state name, locate it on the map, and say one thing they notice about where it is — north, south, coastal, inland.

Class discusses: 'Is there a pattern — do you notice which parts of India have the most dance forms listed?' Teacher draws attention to both the diversity and the spread — pointing out that every region has its own form, and that some regions have several. The section's reference to percussion instruments (dhol, tabla, mridangam, etc.) is connected: each dance form grew alongside local musical traditions.

Students write two observations in their notebooks from the completed map: one about geography (e.g., 'Odissi comes from a coastal state') and one about diversity (e.g., 'No single region holds all the dance forms'). Maps are labelled neatly and kept for reference.

periods.section_context: Classical and folk dance forms of India marked on an India map, states of origin, percussion instruments (dhol, tabla, mridangam, dholak, thavil, idakka, khol, nagara, pakhawaj, dhama, khanjira) as regional cultural products.

periods.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Students identify currency symbols and monuments shown on currency notes by making a table (p. 91)
periods.implied_lo: Students can connect specific national symbols and monuments to the broader idea of a shared national identity built from regional diversity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were designing a new currency note for India, which monument or achievement would you put on it — and would it be from your region or from somewhere else?' This question moves students from observation to genuine reflection on inclusion and shared identity. Allow a range of answers, including those that name lesser-known regional monuments.
materials: A few currency notes of different denominations (teacher's set for display)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures showing monuments on currency notes and the currency symbol identification task

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a brief question: 'India is known for ancient wisdom — like ayurveda and yoga — and also for modern achievements like satellites and digital payments. Can you name one from each?' Students share freely. Teacher notes responses on the board in two columns: 'Ancient heritage' and 'Modern achievement', making the dual nature of India's identity visible.

Students open Textbook p. 91 and make a table in their notebooks listing monuments visible on different currency notes. Teacher displays the notes one denomination at a time, and students identify and record the monument, its approximate location in India, and any detail they know about it. The Indian currency symbol (₹) is also identified as per the Textbook p. 91 task.

Class discusses the connection between the monuments on the notes and the idea of unity in diversity: 'Why would India put monuments from different regions — north, south, east, west — on its currency?' Students connect this to what they observed earlier about regional dance forms spread across the map. Teacher introduces UPI, BHIM, and fast rail networks as examples of India building new connecting systems.

Students write in their notebooks: one ancient Indian contribution and one modern Indian achievement they find most impressive, with one sentence each explaining why. Volunteers share — the class notices the range of choices, reflecting personal connection to different parts of India's story.

periods.section_context: Monuments on currency notes (table), Indian currency symbol (₹), ayurveda, yoga, UPI/BHIM digital payments, fast rail, unity in diversity as threads woven into a shared fabric.

assessment_items.question_text: The white band in the middle of the National Flag of India carries the Ashoka Chakra. What does the white colour of this band stand for?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item checks direct recall of the colour-meaning pairs taught through the textbook passage. Distractors use values that are genuinely associated with India's national identity, making them plausible to students who have partially engaged with the content.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect a national symbol's visual features to the civic values those features represent.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Strength and courage' indicates the student has recalled a value from the flag but assigned it to the wrong colour band — confusing saffron's meaning with white's.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Growth and prosperity' shows the student has recalled green's meaning and displaced it to white — a colour-meaning transposition error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Unity and freedom' suggests the student is drawing on general patriotic vocabulary rather than the specific colour-meaning pairs in the section.

assessment_items.question_text: India adopted its Constitution on 26 January 1950. Give two reasons why having a set of rules for a country — like a Constitution — is important for its citizens.
expected_elements: States that rules / a Constitution ensure fairness or equal treatment for all citizens.
States that rules / a Constitution tell citizens and leaders how the country should be governed or how decisions should be made.
States any other valid civic function: e.g., rules keep people safe, resolve disputes, protect rights. (Any two distinct points accepted.)
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per distinct, relevant reason (maximum 2 marks). Accept responses in the student's own words. Responses that only restate 'because rules are good' without giving a function do not earn the mark.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the purpose of shared rules to the functioning of a community or institution.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

expected_elements: Rules / Constitution ensure fairness or equal treatment for all citizens.
Rules / Constitution guide how the country is governed or how decisions are made.
Any other distinct civic function: keeping people safe, resolving disputes, protecting rights.

assessment_items.question_text: When you look carefully at an Indian currency note, you can find a symbol connected to the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan. What is this symbol, and whose values inspired it?

options.label: A
options.text: A pair of spectacles, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi's values of cleanliness

options.label: B
options.text: Raised dots, inspired by Braille to help visually impaired readers

options.label: C
options.text: The Ashoka Chakra, inspired by Emperor Ashoka's values of dharma

options.label: D
options.text: Three lions, inspired by India's strength and courage

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests whether students engaged with the observation activity closely enough to notice and understand the spectacles symbol. Distractors are drawn directly from other real features of the currency note discussed in the same section, making them diagnostically precise.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations of an everyday object and explain the civic or historical meaning of its design features.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing the Ashoka Chakra suggests the student conflates two national symbols on the note without distinguishing their separate meanings and origins.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing the three lions indicates the student recalled the National Emblem but confused it with the Swachh Bharat symbol — a within-note symbol confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing raised dots shows the student noticed an accessibility feature but misread its purpose, confusing a tactile aid with the civic cleanliness symbol.

assessment_items.task: Design an emblem for your school. In your emblem, include: (a) one symbol or image that shows something you value about your school, (b) a colour that you have chosen deliberately — write one line explaining why you chose it, and (c) a short motto of three to five words.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1 — Choose: What is one important value or quality of your school? Step 2 — Find a symbol: What image, plant, animal, or shape could stand for that value? Step 3 — Choose a colour and write one sentence saying what it means in your emblem. Step 4 — Write your motto: three to five words that express your school's spirit. Step 5 — Draw and colour your emblem neatly.
format_of_output: A drawn and coloured emblem with labelled symbol, chosen colour, written colour explanation, and a motto
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the intentionality of choices, not artistic skill. A strong response shows a deliberate connection between the symbol chosen and the value it represents, a colour explanation that goes beyond 'I like this colour', and a motto that is school-specific rather than generic.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create a symbol-based design that communicates a chosen value or identity through deliberate use of visual elements.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from understanding how national emblems encode meaning to independently applying that same design logic to create a symbol of their own community.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The five-step scaffold separates the thinking (steps 1–3) from the making (steps 4–5), ensuring students plan before drawing. A teacher can check at step 3 whether the reasoning is in place before the student commits to the drawing.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: symbol is specific to the school's context (not a generic star or heart), colour choice has an explained meaning tied to the school's value, motto is short and distinctive. Weak: generic symbols copied from national emblems without adaptation, colour unchosen ('I used blue because it was available'), motto is a copied slogan.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their emblem in words and label its parts. Students who cannot write the motto in English may write it in their home language — the meaning and intention are what matter.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing with written labels and one explanatory sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task mirrors exactly what the textbook activity asks students to do, and the drawn format makes the student's design choices visible for teacher assessment without requiring advanced language.

assessment_items.question_text: Lions once lived across many parts of India. Today they survive only in the Gir forests of Gujarat. Give two reasons why it matters to protect an animal that has been chosen as a national or state symbol.
expected_elements: States that the animal is part of India's natural heritage or biodiversity and its loss would be permanent.
States that national / state symbols represent the identity or pride of the country or state — losing the animal would make the symbol meaningless.

States any other valid conservation or civic reason: e.g., every species plays a role in its ecosystem; protecting one animal often protects the habitat and other species that share it. (Any two distinct points accepted.)
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per distinct, valid reason (maximum 2 marks). Accept responses connecting either ecological value or symbolic/civic value. A response that simply says 'because it is important' without specifying why does not earn the mark.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a guided inquiry to gather specific information and connect findings to a broader environmental or civic question.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: The animal is part of India's natural heritage / biodiversity; its extinction is permanent.
A national or state symbol represents identity and pride — the symbol becomes hollow if the real animal disappears.
Any distinct ecological reason: the animal's role in its food chain / ecosystem; protecting the animal protects its forest habitat.

assessment_items.question_text: Your class made a word-wall showing the word for 'mango' in many different languages. What does this activity best show about India?

options.label: A
options.text: Digital translation apps have replaced the need to learn other languages.

options.label: B
options.text: India has one official language that all citizens must learn.

options.label: C
options.text: India's many languages are a sign of cultural richness and diversity.

options.label: D
options.text: Mango is the national fruit of India.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students drew the intended insight from the activity rather than a surface-level factual recall. Distractors represent misreadings of the section's content that a partially engaged student might hold.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather linguistic data from peers and use it to describe cultural diversity within their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'one official language' directly contradicts the section's content and reveals a misconception about linguistic unity versus linguistic diversity in India.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'mango is the national fruit' shows the student fixated on the example used in the activity (the word 'mango') rather than the concept the activity was illustrating.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing the digital translation option shows the student recalled a detail from the section but misread it as the section's main point, rather than as a supporting tool for linguistic curiosity.

assessment_items.question_text: The textbook uses a forest and a garden to explain India's diversity. A forest has hundreds of different kinds of trees and plants; a garden often has just one or two kinds arranged neatly. Using this comparison, explain how India's diversity of clothing, music, or language makes the country stronger — not weaker.
look_for: Uses the forest-garden comparison clearly — states what makes a diverse forest stronger (resilience, each type playing a role) and maps that quality onto India.
Gives at least one specific example from the chapter's content (headgear from Rajasthan or Himachal Pradesh, a named percussion instrument, a regional language) to ground the argument.
Argues that diversity adds richness or resilience, rather than division — the response does not merely list differences but explains their value.
Writing is organised: the comparison is made before the India example is introduced.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response uses the metaphor as an analytical tool, not just as decoration. Award marks in proportion to: clarity of metaphor use, specificity of example, and strength of the argument that diversity is a source of strength. Accept any chapter-supported example (headgear, dance, instrument, language).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a regional craft or clothing tradition reflects the cultural identity and environment of the community it comes from.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Clear use of the forest-garden metaphor as a comparison tool, not just a mention.
At least one specific example from the chapter: a named headgear style, a percussion instrument, a regional language or dance form.
An argument that diversity adds strength or resilience — not just a list of differences.
Logical organisation: metaphor explained before India example is introduced.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the outline map of India in your mind. A student marked three dance forms on the map: one from a southern coastal state, one from a northern state, and one from an eastern state. What does the spread of dance forms across different parts of India tell us about how culture develops in a country?
expected_elements: States that different regions developed their own distinct cultural practices (dance forms) based on their own history, environment, or community traditions.
States that the spread shows culture is not limited to one part of India — it grew independently and richly in many places.
Any additional valid inference: e.g., no single region 'owns' culture; India's cultural heritage is a product of all its regions together. (Any two distinct points accepted.)
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per distinct, valid inference (maximum 2 marks). The question does not require students to name specific dance forms — it tests whether the map-marking activity led to a genuine geographic and cultural inference. Accept responses that use general regional terms (north, south, east, coast) rather than specific state names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a political map of India to locate and record the regional origins of cultural practices.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

expected_elements: Different regions developed their own distinct cultural practices based on local history, environment, or community traditions.
The spread across north, south, and east shows cultural richness is not limited to one part of India.
Any valid geographic inference: no single region owns India's culture; the spread reflects the country's size and regional variety.

assessment_items.question_text: India's currency notes show monuments from different regions of the country. Why do you think India puts monuments from many different regions on its currency notes rather than showing only one famous monument?

options.label: A
options.text: Because currency notes are printed in different states and each state designs its own note.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the government could not agree on which single monument was most important.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the monuments on notes tell tourists which places to visit in India.

options.label: D
options.text: To show that India's national identity is built from the heritage of all its regions together.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. This item tests whether students moved from observation (naming monuments) to interpretation (understanding why different regions are represented). Distractors represent alternative explanations a student might generate without engaging with the section's core idea of unity in diversity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect specific national symbols and monuments to the broader idea of a shared national identity built from regional diversity.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'could not agree' shows the student applied a conflict-based explanation to a situation the section frames as deliberate inclusion — revealing a gap in understanding the unity-in-diversity concept.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'each state designs its own note' reveals a factual misconception about how currency is issued in India — the student has not engaged with the section's content about the Reserve Bank and national currency design.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'for tourists' shows the student thought of a plausible everyday use for the monuments' images but did not connect it to the civic and national identity purpose the section discusses.
